agree.reason: The low-risk $59 trial, the call with the dietitian, no contract and the honest mixed A1C results make a wary reader willing to try one week, but nothing speaks to why this time would last when other services didn't.

honest.reason: The page drops the 'will lower your A1C' claim and reports the mixed results, but it applies the 0.6 average to the 10 who improved (the brief doesn't say which group it covers), leaves out that medication changes weren't tracked, and calls 10 lunches and dinners 'a week off from carb counting'.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out $12.90 per meal, but it doesn't give the trial's $5.90 per meal or turn 37 of 88 into a 42% six-month retention rate, which is the figure a serial quitter most needs to see.

right_comparison.reason: The only alternative described is counting carbs yourself, and the page doesn't compare the service with the apps and delivery services this reader has already tried and dropped.

qualification.reason: The hedges are general ('can't promise', 'results vary'), with no checkable condition, and they skip the real caveats: 14 customers chose to share results, out of 88, and medication changes weren't tracked.

objections.reason: No contract, meal swaps, the call before starting and the six-month retention figure partly answer 'I'll quit again', but the page never addresses that objection head-on, and the 4-week repeating menu may raise a worry about boredom that it doesn't answer.

fit.reason: It's a clear sales page close to the requested 400 words, with a call to action at the top and bottom that points to the trial order.
